solution.concept_anchor: NPA recognition — 90-day default rule and AQR
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) 'Special Mention Account' is a strong distractor because SMA is the earliest classification in the credit quality continuum and students may confuse SMA-2 (overdue 61–90 days) with NPA (overdue 90+ days), thinking SMA is part of the NPA classification.
elimination_logic: Identify what the set should have in common: the question tests classifications or concepts directly related to NPA measurement under RBI norms.
NPA (Non-Performing Asset), Net NPA, Gross NPA — all directly measure or describe the NPA category.
Special Mention Account (SMA) is a pre-NPA early warning category — it is NOT an NPA. An account becomes SMA-0, SMA-1, or SMA-2 before becoming NPA.
The odd one out is the concept that does NOT represent an actual NPA — SMA is a precursor, not an NPA. Select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: SMA and NPA sit on the same credit quality continuum — SMA is the immediately preceding category before NPA. Students who associate SMA with NPA-related frameworks (which it is) but do not precisely recall that SMA-classified accounts are NOT yet NPAs will include SMA in the NPA group. The distinction: SMA = early warning (performing or recently stressed); NPA = non-performing (90+ days overdue).
solution.final_explanation:
NPA classification in India follows RBI's IRACP (Income Recognition, Asset Classification, and Provisioning) norms, which create distinct categories.

• Option (a) — This belongs: Gross NPA is the total stock of non-performing loans before deducting provisions. It is a core NPA measurement metric.
• Option (b) — This is the odd one out: Special Mention Account (SMA) classifications (SMA-0, SMA-1, SMA-2) flag accounts at early stress stages before they become NPAs. An SMA-2 account is overdue between 61–90 days — once it crosses 90 days without payment, it becomes NPA. SMA is NOT an NPA.
• Option (c) — This belongs: Net NPA (Gross NPA minus provisions) is the PCA trigger metric and a core NPA measurement concept.
• Option (d) — This belongs: 90-day default rule is the NPA recognition norm — an asset becomes NPA when overdue for 90 days or more. It is foundational to NPA classification.

Value Addition:
• SMA-0: overdue 1–30 days; SMA-1: 31–60 days; SMA-2: 61–90 days.
• After 90 days: Sub-standard (first 12 months), then Doubtful, then Loss asset.
• AQR (2015) forced banks to reclassify many restructured accounts as NPAs using this 90-day norm strictly.

solution.concept_anchor: India PCA supervisory vs. US PCA statutory — structural difference

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike the United States, where PCA is mandated by statute under the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Improvement Act (FDICIA) of 1991, India's PCA framework is a regulatory and supervisory tool of the RBI without dedicated statutory backing.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the definitive structural difference between the two frameworks. US PCA is statutory (mandatory by law); India's is administrative/supervisory (RBI's internal tool backed by general statutory powers under Section 35A).

statement_analysis.statement: The United States FDIC's PCA framework classifies banks into three capital categories, mirroring the three threshold levels used in India's PCA framework.
statement_analysis.reason: The US FDIC uses five capital categories (Well Capitalised, Adequately Capitalised, Undercapitalised, Significantly Undercapitalised, Critically Undercapitalised). India uses three threshold levels. The numbers are different — five vs. three.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) claiming Statement 1 is correct and Statement 2 is incorrect is the correct answer (b), not (c) — wait, let me recheck. Statement 1 is correct, Statement 2 is incorrect. The option where Statement 1 is correct and Statement 2 is incorrect maps to option (c). Re-examine: options are (a) both correct, (b) both incorrect, (c) S1 correct S2 incorrect, (d) S1 incorrect S2 correct. Correct mapping is (c).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: US PCA is statutory under FDICIA 1991; India's is supervisory without dedicated legislation. This is the established structural comparison — Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: US FDIC uses five capital categories, not three. India uses three threshold levels. Statement 2 incorrectly assigns three categories to the US framework — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect = option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap in Statement 2 exploits the coincidence of the number three: India has three PCA threshold levels, and students who know this may assume the US system must also use three levels (since PCA inspired India's framework). The US actually uses five capital categories — a fundamentally different granularity. Knowing the US system has five, not three, categories is the precise knowledge point that separates prepared students.
solution.final_explanation:
Comparative analysis of PCA frameworks tests depth beyond domestic knowledge.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The India-US structural distinction is clear. FDICIA 1991 made PCA mandatory for US bank regulators — if a bank falls below a capital threshold, the FDIC must take specified actions by law. In India, PCA is RBI's administrative tool — there is no separate PCA legislation. RBI uses Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act as the legal hook for enforcement.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The US FDIC's PCA framework uses five capital categories: (1) Well Capitalised, (2) Adequately Capitalised, (3) Undercapitalised, (4) Significantly Undercapitalised, (5) Critically Undercapitalised. India's PCA has three threshold levels, not five. The statement's claim that the US uses three categories — matching India's three — is factually wrong.

Correct answer: Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — option (c).

Value Addition:
• FDICIA was a congressional response to the 1980s Savings and Loan crisis that cost US taxpayers ~$130 billion.
• A 'Critically Undercapitalised' US bank must be placed in receivership within 90 days — a more automatic process than India's PCA.
• Basel Committee endorses early intervention frameworks as best practice in Core Principle 11 for effective banking supervision.

solution.concept_anchor: Section 45 — moratorium distinct from PCA invocation
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know Section 35A empowers RBI to issue directions may assume moratorium is also issued under the same section, not distinguishing between operational directions (35A) and moratorium/merger (Section 45).
elimination_logic: Recall that PCA binding directions are issued under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act — this is the general direction-issuing power.
Moratorium involves suspending all bank operations including deposit withdrawals — a far more extreme step requiring a different legislative basis.
Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act specifically authorises RBI to apply to the Central Government for imposing a moratorium on a bank.
Eliminate options pointing to Section 35A, Section 22 (licensing), or Section 11 — none of these govern moratorium.
Select option (c): Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges Section 35A (general direction power used in PCA) with Section 45 (moratorium power). Both sections appear in the Banking Regulation Act and both are RBI supervisory tools. Students who associate 'RBI's authority over distressed banks' uniformly with Section 35A will select option (a). The key distinction: Section 35A allows operational directions while the bank continues functioning; Section 45 enables the extreme step of suspending a bank's operations.
solution.final_explanation:
The Banking Regulation Act provides different sections for different severity levels of RBI intervention — a hierarchy students must know precisely.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Section 35A empowers RBI to issue directions to banks in public interest — this is the provision used for PCA binding directions, restructuring requirements, and operational instructions. It does NOT authorise moratorium.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Section 22 deals with licensing requirements for opening banking companies and branches. It is unrelated to distressed bank intervention.
• Option (c) — Correct: Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act authorises RBI to apply to the Central Government for the imposition of a moratorium on a bank. During moratorium, the bank's operations — including deposit withdrawals — are suspended. This is a depositor-protection emergency measure.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Section 11 relates to minimum paid-up capital requirements for banks. It is a licensing/entry norm, not an intervention mechanism.

Value Addition:
• Intervention continuum: PCA (Section 35A directions) → Moratorium (Section 45) → Forced Merger (Section 45) → Licence Cancellation.
• Yes Bank (2020): Section 45 moratorium imposed, limiting withdrawals to Rs. 50,000 per depositor per month, before SBI-led rescue.
• Moratorium period cannot exceed six months under Section 45.

solution.concept_anchor: Sequence of PCA-related regulatory expansions 2015–2021
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) places the Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act before the AQR, which students might accept if they believe the cooperative bank reforms were part of the same wave as the 2015–16 NPA clean-up.
elimination_logic: Anchor 1: AQR was conducted in 2015–16 — this must precede the 2017 PCA revision.
Anchor 2: The revised PCA framework was announced in 2017 — after AQR, before the 2020 amendment.
Anchor 3: The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act extending RBI powers to UCBs was enacted in 2020.
Anchor 4: PCA extension to NBFCs and Small Finance Banks occurred in 2021.
Correct order: AQR (2015–16) → Revised PCA (2017) → BR Amendment for UCBs (2020) → NBFC PCA (2021). Select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal trap attempts to swap the 2017 PCA revision with the 2020 Banking Regulation amendment — both are regulatory reforms occurring in quick succession. Students who associate banking sector reform 'waves' may cluster the 2017 revision with the 2015–16 AQR but may not recall that the UCB reform came three years later in 2020, and the NBFC extension was a year after that in 2021.
solution.final_explanation:
Sequencing RBI's supervisory expansions tests the ability to distinguish between closely spaced reforms.

Correct sequence:
1. AQR (2015–16): RBI compelled banks to recognise hidden NPAs, triggering PCA placements for multiple PSBs.
2. Revised PCA framework (2017): Updated thresholds and indicators; coincided with peak NPA crisis.
3. Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act (2020): Extended RBI supervisory jurisdiction to Urban Cooperative Banks — a significant expansion.
4. PCA extended to NBFCs and Small Finance Banks (2021): Largest scope expansion of PCA in its history.

Wrong options:
• Option (b) swaps events 1 and 2 — places UCB amendment before AQR, which reverses the causal sequence.
• Option (c) places NBFC extension before UCB amendment — factually reversed.
• Option (d) places 2017 revision last — contradicted by the 2020 and 2021 events which post-date it.

Value Addition:
• UCB: Urban Cooperative Banks; oversight had a regulatory gap before 2020 — multiple UCB failures (PMC Bank 2019) prompted the amendment.
• PMC Bank crisis (2019) accelerated the push for RBI oversight of UCBs via the 2020 amendment.
• 2021 represents the most comprehensive regulatory perimeter around PCA — covering commercial banks, SFBs, UCBs, and major NBFCs.

solution.concept_anchor: BFS composition — RBI Governor as Chairman
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because it describes a plausible-sounding governance body ('RBI Deputy Governor for Supervision as Chairman') that sounds more operationally logical — students may think the Deputy Governor for banking supervision would chair BFS, not the Governor.
elimination_logic: Option (a): BFS as RBI's monetary policy committee — incorrect; MPC is a separate statutory body. BFS is a supervisory body.
Option (b): BFS chaired by Finance Secretary — incorrect; BFS is chaired by the RBI Governor, not a government official.
Option (c): BFS chaired by RBI Governor + four co-opted directors from RBI Central Board — this is the actual composition. Correct.
Option (d): Deputy Governor for Supervision as Chairman — plausible but wrong; the RBI Governor is Chairman.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The plausible-fabrication trap in option (d) exploits operational logic: the Deputy Governor responsible for banking supervision handles day-to-day regulatory work, making it seem natural that they would chair BFS. But BFS is a board-level supervisory oversight body, chaired by the RBI Governor personally, reflecting its status as the highest internal supervisory oversight forum. Students who rely on logical inference rather than factual recall will select option (d).
solution.final_explanation:
BFS composition is a precise factual recall question with a plausible trap.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Describing BFS as RBI's monetary policy committee is wrong on two counts — BFS is a supervisory body, not a policy body; and the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) is the monetary policy body, which is a separate statutory committee under the RBI Act.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Finance Secretary has no role in BFS. BFS is entirely internal to the RBI. Government officials do not sit on BFS.
• Option (c) — Correct: BFS is chaired by the RBI Governor. It includes four directors co-opted from RBI's Central Board (typically non-official directors). The Deputy Governor in charge of banking supervision serves as its Vice-Chairman. Meets at least monthly.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: While the Deputy Governor for Supervision serves as Vice-Chairman, the Chairman is the RBI Governor — not the Deputy Governor. This is the precise trap in this question.

Value Addition:
• BFS constituted in November 1994 on the recommendation of the Narasimham Committee on Financial System.
• BFS oversees: commercial banks, UCBs, NBFCs, FIs such as NABARD, NHB, SIDBI, EXIM Bank.
• BFS is distinct from FSDC (Financial Stability and Development Council), which is a government-chaired inter-regulatory body.

PCA and Its Impact on Public Sector Banks: Structural Vulnerability

solution.concept_anchor: PCA limitations — government dual role and regulatory forbearance

statement_analysis.statement: A structural criticism of the PCA framework as applied to public sector banks is that the government's dual role — as bank owner providing recapitalization and as the political authority over the banking regulator — creates tensions that can dilute PCA's effectiveness.
statement_analysis.reason: This is a well-documented governance tension. The government's ownership interest in PSBs creates pressure to dilute regulatory strictness, as seen in the 2018 RBI-Government standoff over PCA restrictions.

statement_analysis.statement: Regulatory forbearance — the delayed recognition of NPAs by banks with implicit or explicit regulatory tolerance — can cause banks to enter the PCA framework only after their financial stress has become severe, reducing PCA's value as an early corrective tool.
statement_analysis.reason: Regulatory forbearance is a documented limitation of PCA. Banks that evergreen loans or delay NPA classification appear healthy until suddenly stressed, entering PCA at a late stage when corrective options are limited.

statement_analysis.statement: Empirical evidence conclusively demonstrates that the PCA framework has successfully resolved all cases of bank stress in India, eliminating the need for any bank rescue or government capital injection after PCA placement.
statement_analysis.reason: No such conclusive evidence exists. PCA is critiqued for managing rather than fully resolving bank stress — capital injections have continued even for banks that eventually exited PCA, and some banks required multiple rounds of recapitalization.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) claiming all three correct is a strong distractor because Statements 1 and 2 represent credible, nuanced critiques that a well-prepared student will recognise as accurate, making it tempting to extend that accuracy to Statement 3.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Government dual role creating governance tension — this is the documented RBI-Government 2018 conflict. Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Regulatory forbearance causing delayed PCA entry — this is supported by the AQR experience showing banks had hidden NPAs for years. Statement 2 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 3: 'Conclusively demonstrates' + 'eliminating the need for any rescue' — the absolute language makes this false; PCA has managed but not fully resolved bank stress in all cases. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Only Statements 1 and 2 correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses the scope-extension technique with the words 'conclusively' and 'eliminating the need for any bank rescue or government capital injection after PCA placement.' Both qualifiers make the statement demonstrably false — banks continued to receive capital injections even while under or after PCA. Students who read quickly and only notice 'PCA has successfully resolved bank stress' (without catching 'conclusively' and 'all cases') may accept Statement 3.
solution.final_explanation:
The limitations and criticisms of PCA constitute important UPSC Mains material that also appears in Prelims.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The government's dual role is a genuine structural tension. As owner of PSBs, the government wants them to lend (especially pre-election); as the authority above the regulator, it can exert pressure to relax PCA. The 2018 standoff, which contributed to then-Governor Urjit Patel's departure, exemplifies this tension.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Regulatory forbearance — allowing banks to roll over bad loans ('evergreening') without classifying them as NPAs — keeps banks below PCA triggers artificially. The AQR forced recognition, causing a sudden spike. This means PCA functioned as a lagged, reactive tool in the 2015–18 cycle, not an early preventive one.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: PCA has not 'conclusively' resolved all bank stress or eliminated capital injections. Banks like Bank of India and UCO Bank exited PCA but continued to receive government capital support. PCA manages the deterioration — it does not guarantee recovery.

Value Addition:
• 'Evergreening' of loans: rolling over a defaulting loan as a new loan to avoid NPA classification.
• IMF FSAP noted India's PCA as reactive rather than fully preventive.
• The 2018 RBI-Government conflict: government sought Section 7 of RBI Act consultation to override RBI on PCA relaxation — historically unprecedented.

solution.concept_anchor: NBFC PCA — government NBFCs excluded from coverage
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who know NBFCs are now under PCA assume government ownership provides no exception, not realising that government NBFCs are explicitly carved out.
elimination_logic: Identify that the entity is a government-owned NBFC — this is the key feature that determines PCA applicability.
Recall that government NBFCs are explicitly excluded from the NBFC PCA framework.
Eliminate option (a): Mandatory restrictions on dividend payment would apply if the NBFC were under PCA — but government NBFCs are excluded, so PCA does not apply.
Eliminate option (b): PCA does cover many NBFCs but government NBFCs are specifically excluded — this option ignores the government ownership carve-out.
Eliminate option (c): The Rs. 2 lakh deposit ceiling is the Payments Bank rule — irrelevant to a government NBFC.
Select option (d): Government NBFCs are explicitly excluded from the NBFC PCA framework.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap works in both directions here: students who over-generalise 'NBFCs are now under PCA' (true for most) to 'all NBFCs are under PCA' (false — government NBFCs are excluded) will select option (b). The government NBFC exclusion is logical (sovereign backing reduces systemic risk from these entities) but requires specific recall of the exclusion list.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario tests the specific exclusion carve-outs within the NBFC PCA framework.

Applicable principle: The 2021 NBFC PCA framework explicitly excludes government-owned NBFCs from its coverage. The rationale is that implicit or explicit sovereign backing reduces the systemic risk associated with their failure — they are unlikely to require the same structured corrective intervention as market-owned NBFCs.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: If the NBFC were under PCA, dividend prohibition would indeed apply. But since government NBFCs are excluded, this option is based on a false premise about PCA applicability.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: While the statement about PCA covering NBFCs is broadly true, the scenario involves a government NBFC — which is among the specific categories excluded. Applying PCA to it would exceed the framework's stated scope.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Rs. 2 lakh deposit ceiling applies to Payments Banks — completely unrelated to an NBFC's regulatory classification or PCA status.
• Option (d) — Correct: Government-owned NBFCs are explicitly excluded from the NBFC PCA framework. The RBI circular extending PCA to NBFCs (2021) specifically carves out government NBFCs, along with Primary Dealers and Housing Finance Companies under NHB.

Value Addition:
• Government NBFC examples: NABARD (technically classified differently), Indian Infrastructure Finance Company Limited (IIFCL), Power Finance Corporation (PFC).
• PFC and REC are government NBFCs that carry sovereign backing — their exclusion from PCA is consistent with their risk profile.
• NHB regulates HFCs separately — that is why HFCs under NHB are also excluded from RBI's NBFC PCA.

solution.concept_anchor: PCA trigger thresholds — exact numerical values

statement_analysis.statement: A bank whose CRAR falls below 10.25% breaches PCA Threshold 1 for the capital adequacy indicator.
statement_analysis.reason: 10.25% is the Threshold 1 CRAR trigger under PCA — set above the 9% regulatory minimum to incorporate the Capital Conservation Buffer.

statement_analysis.statement: A bank whose Net NPA ratio exceeds 10% has breached PCA Threshold 1 but not Threshold 2 for the asset quality indicator.
statement_analysis.reason: Net NPA above 10% breaches Threshold 2, not just Threshold 1. Threshold 1 is Net NPA above 6%; Threshold 2 is Net NPA above 9% (approximate figures per the revised framework). A bank at 10% Net NPA is beyond Threshold 1.

statement_analysis.statement: Multiple simultaneous threshold breaches across different indicators can escalate the severity of PCA restrictions applied to a bank.
statement_analysis.reason: The PCA framework is designed so that breaching thresholds on multiple indicators simultaneously escalates the severity of interventions, reflecting the compounded risk profile.

statement_analysis.statement: Under PCA, a bank that has breached Threshold 3 across all three indicators may be recommended for forced merger or license cancellation by the RBI.
statement_analysis.reason: Threshold 3 is the most severe PCA level — at this point, RBI may escalate beyond PCA restrictions to consider forced merger under Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act or even license cancellation.

solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Only three' is the strong distractor because pairs 1, 3, and 4 are all correct, making 'Only three' seem natural — students may miss that pair 2 contains a nuanced but clear error about the threshold level corresponding to Net NPA above 10%.
elimination_logic: Pair 1: CRAR below 10.25% triggers Threshold 1 — correct.
Pair 2: Net NPA above 10% = Threshold 1 only — incorrect. Net NPA above 6% is Threshold 1; above 9% escalates to Threshold 2. A 10% Net NPA breaches Threshold 2, not merely Threshold 1.
Pair 3: Multiple simultaneous breaches escalate severity — correct.
Pair 4: Threshold 3 breach across all indicators → possible forced merger or cancellation — correct.
Three pairs correct (1, 3, 4); one incorrect (2). Select option (c) 'Only three.'
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap in pair 2 exploits imprecise knowledge of threshold gradation. 'Net NPA above 10% has breached Threshold 1 but not Threshold 2' contains a half-truth: such a bank HAS breached Threshold 1 (since above 6% qualifies). But it has also breached Threshold 2 (since above 9% qualifies). The statement's claim that it is 'not Threshold 2' is false. Students who only recall 'Threshold 1 = above 6%' without knowing Threshold 2 values will accept pair 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Precise knowledge of PCA threshold values is tested here with a partial-truth trap on gradation.

Pair 1 — Correct: CRAR below 10.25% triggers Threshold 1. This is the capital adequacy early-warning trigger under PCA.
Pair 2 — Incorrect: Net NPA above 10% has breached BOTH Threshold 1 (trigger: above 6%) and Threshold 2 (trigger: above 9%). The statement's claim that it is 'not Threshold 2' is wrong — a bank with 10% Net NPA has crossed both lower thresholds and sits at or near Threshold 2.
Pair 3 — Correct: Simultaneous multi-indicator breaches reflect compounded distress and escalate the severity of PCA interventions imposed.
Pair 4 — Correct: Threshold 3 is the highest severity level under PCA. At this stage, standard PCA restrictions are insufficient and RBI may recommend escalation to forced merger or license cancellation under Section 45.

Three of the four pairs (1, 3, 4) are correct — answer is 'Only three.'

Value Addition:
• Threshold 1 Net NPA trigger: above 6%; Threshold 2: above 9%; Threshold 3: above 12% (approximate revised figures).
• Threshold 3 CRAR trigger: below 6.75% (approximate — significantly below the 9% minimum, indicating near-insolvency).
• Even at Threshold 3, PCA does not automatically terminate the bank — RBI still assesses resolution options.

solution.concept_anchor: PCA credit flow impact — MSME, priority sector, systemic risk

statement_analysis.statement: The simultaneous placement of a large number of public sector banks under PCA in 2018 had a systemic effect on credit availability, particularly affecting borrowers reliant on PSB lending such as small enterprises and unrated businesses.
statement_analysis.reason: 11 PSBs under PCA simultaneously in 2018 contracted collective credit capacity significantly, disproportionately affecting small and unrated borrowers who relied primarily on PSB credit channels.

statement_analysis.statement: Priority sector lending obligations of a bank are automatically waived for the entire duration that the bank remains under PCA.
statement_analysis.reason: PCA does not automatically waive priority sector lending (PSL) obligations. PSL targets remain in force for PCA banks — though their reduced lending capacity may affect compliance and attract RIDF contributions as penalty.

statement_analysis.statement: The government's argument during the 2018 RBI-PCA conflict was that PCA restrictions were preventing banks from adequately financing large infrastructure projects and thereby slowing GDP growth.
statement_analysis.reason: The government's primary argument was about credit restriction to MSMEs and small borrowers, not specifically about large infrastructure projects. Large infrastructure projects typically access capital markets and development finance institutions — the MSME credit constraint was the core political concern.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) pointing only to Statement 2 as incorrect is a strong distractor because Statement 2 is clearly incorrect (PSL waiver), but students may not carefully read Statement 3 and assume its imprecise description of the government's argument is close enough to be correct.
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1: Systemic credit squeeze from simultaneous PCA of 11 PSBs — well documented. Statement 1 is correct.
Test Statement 2: PSL obligations automatically waived under PCA — this is false; PSL targets remain. Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Test Statement 3: Government's 2018 argument was about MSME credit, not primarily large infrastructure. Statement 3 mischaracterises the government's argument — it is NOT correct.
Statements 2 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3's trap is in the precision of the government's argument: the 2018 conflict centred on MSME credit restriction, not large infrastructure. Infrastructure projects typically access bond markets, NaBFID/DFI channels, and large private banks — not primarily PCA-bound PSBs. Students who recall 'government criticised PCA for restricting credit' without the specific MSME focus will accept Statement 3 as accurate.
solution.final_explanation:
The credit flow dimension of PCA connects to political economy and sectoral impact — important for both Prelims and Mains.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 2018 simultaneous PCA placement of 11 PSBs was a systemic event. PSBs collectively account for 60%+ of banking system credit, and their constrained lending disproportionately affected MSMEs and unrated borrowers who cannot access capital markets or private banks as easily.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect (this is one answer): Priority sector lending (PSL) targets — for agriculture, MSMEs, export credit, etc. — are NOT waived under PCA. Banks under PCA must still meet PSL targets. If they fall short, they contribute to RBI's Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) or other specified funds as a penalty mechanism.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect (this is the second answer): The government's specific concern in 2018 was about MSME credit — small and medium enterprises that depend heavily on PSB branches for working capital finance. The argument was not primarily about large infrastructure (which has its own financing channels), but about the micro-credit and MSME segment.

Value Addition:
• PSL target: 40% of adjusted net bank credit (ANBC) for domestic scheduled commercial banks.
• RIDF contribution: mandatory for banks falling short of PSL targets — interest rate penalty.
• The 2018 RBI-Government standoff involved invocation of Section 7 of the RBI Act — unprecedented in independent India's history.
